name: Bingo (Dominoes)
description: Bingo is a historic domino trick-taking game for 2 players based on the card game Sixty-Six. Hailed as the 'king of domino games' in 19th-century America, it features a unique hierarchy where the double-blank tile, named 'Bingo', is the supreme trump. Players win tricks to collect point-values from the tiles, aiming to reach 70 points and claim the deal. This game predates the popular lottery-style Bingo and represents a high-skill adaptation of card mechanics to dominoes.

history.origins: Developed in 19th-century America as a response to religious prohibitions on playing cards. Trick-taking card games like Sixty-Six were adapted to use domino tiles, with 'Bingo' emerging as the most complex and respected of these variants.
timeline: 1868: First described by William Brisbane Dick in 'Hoyle's Games'.
1880s: Widely played in the American South and Midwest.
1920s: Declines in popularity as card-playing taboos fade.
Present: A rare specialty game studied by domino historians and hobbyists.
history.cultural: A unique cultural artifact showing the adaptability of card game engines to alternative components when social or religious constraints applied.
history.evolution: The game essentially mirrors the mechanics of Sixty-Six (or 66), including the 'Closing' mechanic and the 'Marriage' (double) equivalents.

setup.dealing: Tiles are shuffled face-down. Each player draws 7 tiles. The remaining 14 tiles form the face-down stock.

rules.objective: Win tricks worth at least 70 points to win the deal and accumulate 7 game points to win the match.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Start**: The first tile played determines the trump suit (Blanks). 2. **Tricks**: Players play one tile each. Highest trump wins; if no trump, highest card of led suit wins. 3. **The Draw**: While the stock exists, players draw one tile after each trick. 4. **Trump**: The double-blank (Bingo) is the highest trump, followed by other tiles with blanks. 5. **Closing**: A player may 'close the stock' to stop drawing and force strict suit-following.
keyRules: The double-blank (Bingo) tile beats all other tiles.
Any tile with a blank end counts as a trump.
Suit-following is only mandatory after the stock is closed or empty.
You must actively claim victory once you reach 70 points.

strategy.basic: Prioritize winning tricks that contain high-value doubles (6-6 is 12 points, 5-5 is 10 points). These are the 'Volle' of the game.
strategy.intermediate: Counting: There are only 28 tiles. Track which trumps have been played to know if your Bingo is the last remaining master tile.
strategy.advanced: Closing the Stock: If you have a strong hand of trumps and believe you can reach 70 points without drawing more, close the stock. This forces your opponent to follow suit, potentially trapping their high-value doubles.
tips: Don't lead your best trumps early; save them to capture your opponent's high doubles.
If you win a trick and draw a blank tile, you've gained a trump.

variations.name: Single Point Bingo
variations.description: A simplified version where every deal is worth exactly 1 point, ignoring the margin of victory.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: This variant only changes how many game points are awarded per deal; the core engine and progression remain the same.

scoring.description: Win tricks worth at least 70 points. Game points: 1 (loser has 30+), 2 (loser has <30), 3 (loser won 0 tricks). Match to 7 game points.
scoring.winCondition: First to 7 game points across multiple deals.

synthesis.shortDescription: A 19th-century American domino trick-taking game adapted from Sixty-Six. Two players duel with tiles, winning tricks for points. The double-blank — 'Bingo' — is the unconquerable trump. Collect 70 points, claim victory, and score game points. Once hailed as the most skilful domino game ever devised.
